name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: The supplied evidence does not describe a strong disease pattern, but hidden or early problems are still possible.
next_steps: Inspect both leaf surfaces and new growth weekly.
Compare several leaves rather than relying on one photo.
prevention: Prune for airflow and remove fallen diseased leaves.
Avoid unnecessary leaf wetness.

name: Apple scab pattern
overview: Apple scab commonly produces olive-to-dark lesions that may distort leaves and fruit in wet weather.
next_steps: Check young leaves and fruit for velvety olive lesions.
Remove heavily affected fallen material and seek local guidance if fruit is involved.
prevention: Open the canopy to improve drying.
Clear fallen leaves that can carry inoculum.

name: Cedar-apple rust pattern
overview: Cedar-apple rust often creates bright yellow-orange spots followed by darker structures on leaf undersides.
next_steps: Inspect leaf undersides for orange structures.
Ask a local extension service to distinguish rust from other leaf spots.
prevention: Use resistant cultivars where practical.
Improve airflow and monitor nearby alternate hosts.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: No strong disease pattern is described; continue monitoring because nutrient and weather stress can emerge quickly.
next_steps: Inspect leaves at several canopy levels.
Record changes after irrigation or weather events.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue appropriately.
Use locally adapted seed and balanced nutrition.

name: Common rust pattern
overview: Common rust typically produces cinnamon-to-orange raised pustules on both leaf surfaces.
next_steps: Rub a suspected pustule gently and look for rust-coloured residue.
Estimate how much of the canopy is affected before taking action.
prevention: Choose resistant hybrids.
Monitor fields during cool, humid periods.

name: Northern leaf blight pattern
overview: Northern leaf blight commonly causes long, gray-green to tan cigar-shaped lesions.
next_steps: Look for elongated lesions rather than small round spots.
Seek agronomic advice if lesions reach upper leaves before flowering.
prevention: Rotate away from corn where pressure is high.
Manage infected residue and use resistant hybrids.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: The supplied evidence does not describe a strong cucumber disease pattern.
next_steps: Inspect the underside of older and newer leaves.
Monitor vines for rapid changes after humid weather.
prevention: Water at soil level and provide airflow.
Remove badly damaged leaves without over-pruning.

name: Powdery mildew pattern
overview: Powdery mildew appears as white powdery patches that expand across leaf surfaces.
next_steps: Check whether the white material sits on the surface and spreads in patches.
Separate badly affected leaves and confirm locally before treatment.
prevention: Increase spacing and airflow.
Avoid excessive nitrogen that creates dense tender growth.

name: Downy mildew pattern
overview: Downy mildew often causes angular yellow lesions bounded by leaf veins, with darker growth underneath.
next_steps: Look for angular lesions limited by veins and inspect leaf undersides early in the day.
Escalate quickly if symptoms are spreading across vines.
prevention: Keep foliage dry and improve airflow.
Remove volunteer cucurbits and use resistant varieties when available.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: No strong disease pattern is described in the submitted grape evidence.
next_steps: Inspect leaves, shoots, and fruit clusters separately.
Monitor after rainfall.
prevention: Maintain an open canopy.
Remove mummified fruit and infected debris.

name: Black rot pattern
overview: Black rot can produce tan leaf spots with dark margins and shrivelled dark fruit.
next_steps: Inspect fruit clusters for shrivelling and tiny black structures.
Remove mummified fruit and seek vineyard advice if clusters are affected.
prevention: Prune for airflow and sanitation.
Remove infected fruit and canes during dormancy.

name: Powdery mildew pattern
overview: Grape powdery mildew creates white-gray surface growth on leaves, shoots, or berries.
next_steps: Check young leaves and berries for surface growth.
Confirm before treatment because spray residue can look similar.
prevention: Open the canopy and avoid dense shaded growth.
Use locally recommended resistant cultivars.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: The evidence does not form a strong pepper disease pattern.
next_steps: Inspect new leaves and fruit for small lesions.
Monitor watering and nutrient consistency.
prevention: Use clean seed or transplants.
Avoid working with wet plants.

name: Bacterial spot pattern
overview: Bacterial spot often causes small water-soaked lesions that darken and may develop yellow halos.
next_steps: Check whether older lesions tear out and leave shot holes.
Avoid handling wet plants and seek confirmation if fruit is spotted.
prevention: Use clean planting material.
Rotate crops and reduce overhead irrigation.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: No strong potato disease pattern is described.
next_steps: Inspect lower canopy leaves and stems.
Monitor after cool, wet weather.
prevention: Use certified seed potatoes.
Rotate crops and destroy volunteer potatoes.

name: Early blight pattern
overview: Early blight commonly starts on older leaves as dark target-like spots with concentric rings.
next_steps: Look for target-like rings on older leaves.
Confirm whether lesions are dry rather than water-soaked.
prevention: Rotate crops and remove infected debris.
Reduce plant stress with consistent water and nutrition.

name: Late blight pattern
overview: Late blight may create rapidly expanding water-soaked lesions and pale growth beneath leaves in cool, wet weather.
next_steps: Isolate suspect plants and inspect leaf undersides at lesion margins.
Contact a local agricultural advisor promptly because late blight can spread rapidly.
prevention: Use certified seed and eliminate volunteer potatoes.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness and monitor regional alerts.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: The evidence does not describe a strong strawberry disease pattern.
next_steps: Inspect crowns, fruit, and leaf undersides.
Monitor after humid periods.
prevention: Use clean transplants and good spacing.
Keep fruit and leaves away from wet soil.

name: Leaf scorch pattern
overview: Leaf scorch can cause many small purple spots that merge into brown, scorched tissue.
next_steps: Check whether many small spots merge along leaf margins.
Remove heavily affected old foliage after confirmation.
prevention: Improve airflow and avoid overhead watering.
Renovate beds and remove infected debris appropriately.

name: Powdery mildew pattern
overview: Powdery mildew may cause white surface growth, upward leaf curl, and reddish-purple patches.
next_steps: Inspect leaf undersides and fruit for powdery growth.
Confirm that the pale coating is not dust or spray residue.
prevention: Use good spacing and ventilation.
Choose resistant cultivars where available.

name: No obvious disease pattern
overview: No strong tomato disease pattern is described, though early symptoms and non-disease stress remain possible.
next_steps: Inspect new growth, lower leaves, stems, and fruit.
Track changes with photos taken in similar lighting.
prevention: Water consistently at soil level.
Provide spacing, support, and balanced nutrition.

name: Early blight pattern
overview: Early blight usually begins on older leaves with brown target-like spots and surrounding yellowing.
next_steps: Look for concentric rings on lower leaves and lesions near the soil line.
Remove severely affected lower leaves after confirmation and avoid splashing soil.
prevention: Mulch to reduce soil splash.
Rotate crops and improve airflow.

name: Late blight pattern
overview: Late blight can cause rapidly expanding, greasy water-soaked lesions and pale growth below leaves.
next_steps: Separate suspect plants and inspect lesion margins and leaf undersides.
Contact a local plant-health service promptly because this pattern can spread rapidly.
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness.
Remove volunteer solanaceous plants and monitor local alerts.

name: Septoria leaf spot pattern
overview: Septoria often produces numerous small circular spots with pale centres and dark margins on lower leaves.
next_steps: Use magnification to look for tiny black dots in pale lesion centres.
Compare with early blight; Septoria spots usually lack target-like rings.
prevention: Mulch and water at the base.
Remove infected debris and rotate crops.

name: Bacterial spot pattern
overview: Bacterial spot may produce small water-soaked lesions on leaves and raised spots on fruit.
next_steps: Inspect fruit and young leaves for small raised or water-soaked spots.
Avoid handling wet plants and obtain confirmation before management.
prevention: Use clean seed and transplants.
Reduce overhead irrigation and rotate crops.

name: Yellow leaf curl virus pattern
overview: Yellow leaf curl virus commonly causes upward curling, yellowed young leaves, and stunted growth.
next_steps: Inspect young growth for stunting and check nearby plants for whiteflies.
Seek confirmation because herbicide injury and nutrient stress can look similar.
prevention: Use virus-resistant varieties where available.
Manage weeds and insect vectors using locally appropriate integrated methods.

name: Leaf mold pattern
overview: Leaf mold often causes yellow patches above and olive-gray velvety growth below leaves in humid protected spaces.
next_steps: Compare upper yellow patches with olive-gray growth on the underside.
Lower humidity and confirm before removing extensive foliage.
prevention: Ventilate protected growing areas.
Space plants and avoid wetting foliage.
